## Plugin reference

- Description: Global toast notifications: a plain showToast() (text toasts: data only) backed by sonner's global API, and useShowCustomToast() — a toast whose content the caller draws, rendered in the caller's render origin (its transport, registry and navigator) while the stack only places it, plus the Core.Root-mounted sonner Toaster host. Degrades to a silent no-op when no host is mounted. A toast declaring audience developer is shown only in Developer mode. A custom toast states why it is shown: an announcement (something that happened on its own, e.g. a notification arriving) is raised only on a page on screen and always leaves after the announcement duration, whatever its variant; a reply (the answer to the user's own action) stays as long as its caller says, Infinity included. useSuppressToasts() lets a surface that is its whole document (the menu-bar panel) turn the host off while mounted.

## Announcements vs replies: the kind owns the lifetime

A toast is either a **reply** — the answer to something the user did (Copied, a
failed save: raised whatever the page's state, the user is waiting for it) — or
an **announcement** of something that happened on its own (a notification
arriving, the server reconnecting). The caller states which (`kind`), never an
announcement's lifetime:

- **An announcement is raised only while the page is on screen**
  (`isPageOnScreen`, checked by `showToast` / `useShowCustomToast` themselves),
  and **leaves after `ANNOUNCEMENT_DURATION_MS` (4 s) whatever its variant** —
  a custom announcement has no `duration` field to set. Its record lives on its
  persistent surface (the bell's row and unread badge), so nothing is lost.
- **A reply** (`kind: "reply"`, the text default) is shown whatever the page's
  state; a custom reply states its `duration` (`Infinity` keeps it until
  handled — an error answering the user's own action).
- A text toast is never sticky: it takes sonner's default lifetime, whatever
  its variant.

Why the hidden-page gate: sonner pauses every toast's dismiss timer while the
document is hidden and keeps every toast in its list mounted (only the front
three are drawn), so a toast raised in a hidden tab stays until the tab is
shown. Before this rule a background tab kept one toast per notification.
Measured per arrival on a hidden page: +35 DOM nodes, +28 layout objects, +146
event listeners (each custom toast is its own React root). On 2026-11-14 that
added ~12k nodes per tab in 2 h and took one Chrome renderer with 6 equin tabs
from 3.3 GB to 10.4 GB (report-1794679800-lyevgy).

Why no sticky announcement: an error arrival used to stay until dismissed, so a
tab left ON screen kept every one (~20 error notifications an hour on main,
mostly developer reports). Measured on a visible tab by
`shell/notifications/e2e/arrival-toast-leak.ts`: per error arrival +252 KB app
heap, +146 listeners, +39 DOM nodes, every toast still mounted; after, 4.9 KB,
0 nodes, 0 listeners (PASS).

## A dismissed toast keeps nothing

sonner keeps its last ~100 toasts' JSX in its history after they are dismissed.
A custom toast's JSX therefore reaches its content — the adopted element, and
through it the detached `<li>`, the content's DOM and its React listeners —
only through one reference (`live` in `showCustomToast`) released when the body
unmounts for good, and the content is built in its own function
(`raiseContent`) so no closure the JSX holds shares its scope. Without that,
each dismissed custom toast kept ~58 KB, 7 DOM nodes and ~143 listeners until
100 later toasts pushed it out.

## Click-to-dismiss

Clicking a toast anywhere dismisses it — except a click that ends a text
selection (so its words can be copied), and a click on a control inside it (a
button, link or input: its action, a custom toast's ×, a popover trigger),
which is the control's own: it acts, and dismisses itself if it means to. The
check runs in the body's native `<li>` listener (`isControlClick`), not by the
control stopping propagation, which from React would come too late.
